A '''welfare state''' is a form of government in which the [[State (polity)|state]] (or a well-established network of social institutions) protects and promotes the economic and social [[well-being]] of its citizens, based upon the principles of [[equal opportunity]], equitable [[distribution of wealth]], and public responsibility for citizens unable to avail themselves of the minimal provisions for a good life.<ref name="britannica">{{cite encyclopedia| url= http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/639266/welfare-state |title= Welfare state| encyclopedia= [[Britannica Online Encyclopedia]]|date= 18 November 2023}}</ref>

There is substantial variability in the form and trajectory of the welfare state across countries and regions.<ref name="Béland-2021a">{{Citation|last1=Béland|first1=Daniel|title=Introduction|date=2021|url=https://oxfordhandbooks.com/view/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198828389.001.0001/oxfordhb-9780198828389-e-1|work=The Oxford Handbook of the Welfare State|pages=xxx–20|editor-last=Béland|editor-first=Daniel|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=en|doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198828389.013.1|isbn=978-0-19-882838-9|last2=Morgan|first2=Kimberly J.|last3=Obinger|first3=Herbert|last4=Pierson|first4=Christopher|editor2-last=Leibfried|editor2-first=Stephan|editor3-last=Morgan|editor3-first=Kimberly J.|editor4-last=Obinger|editor4-first=Herbert|url-access=subscription}}</ref> All welfare states entail some degree of [[Public–private partnership|private–public partnerships]] wherein the administration and delivery of at least some welfare programs occur through private entities.<ref name="Béland-2021b">{{Citation|last1=Béland|first1=Daniel|title=Governance|date=2021|url=https://oxfordhandbooks.com/view/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198828389.001.0001/oxfordhb-9780198828389-e-10|work=The Oxford Handbook of the Welfare State|pages=172–187|editor-last=Béland|editor-first=Daniel|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=en|doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198828389.013.10|isbn=978-0-19-882838-9|last2=Morgan|first2=Kimberly J.|editor2-last=Leibfried|editor2-first=Stephan|editor3-last=Morgan|editor3-first=Kimberly J.|editor4-last=Obinger|editor4-first=Herbert|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Welfare state services are also provided at varying territorial levels of government.<ref name="Béland-2021b"/>

The contemporary capitalist welfare state has been described as a type of [[mixed economy]] in the sense of state interventionism, as opposed to a mixture of planning and markets, since [[economic planning]] was not a key feature or component of the welfare state.<ref name= "EPE1247">{{cite encyclopedia|title=Welfare state|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Political Economy|editor-first=Phillip Anthony|editor-last=O'Hara|publisher=Routledge|year= 1999|page=1247|isbn= 0-415-24187-1|quote=The welfare state emerged in the twentieth century as one institutional form of this socially protective response. In the 1930s, the responses of emerging welfare states to the Great Depression were to the immediate circumstances of massive unemployment, lost output, and collapse of the financial and trading systems. Planning was not a key element in the response to the crisis of capitalism. Instead, the character of welfare state intervention can best be described as an 'interventionist drift', reflecting the spontaneous, uncoordinated reactions of the protective response.}}</ref> Early features therein, such as public pensions and social insurance, developed from the 1880s onwards in industrializing Western countries.<ref name="Skocpol-1992">{{Cite book|url=https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674717664|title=Protecting Soldiers and Mothers|last=Skocpol|first=Theda|date=1992|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-71766-4 |language=en|access-date=21 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="Béland-2021a"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koehler-Derrick |first1=Gabriel |last2=Lee |first2=Melissa M. |date=2023 |title=War and Welfare in Colonial Algeria |journal=International Organization |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=263–293 |language=en |doi=10.1017/S0020818322000376 |s2cid=256724058 |issn=0020-8183|doi-access=free }}</ref> World War I, the [[Great Depression]], and World War II have been characterized as important events that ushered in the expansion of the welfare state.<ref name="Skocpol-1992"/><ref name="WF EPE2">{{cite encyclopedia|year=1999|title=Welfare state|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Political Economy|publisher=Routledge|editor-last=O'Hara|editor-first=Phillip Anthony|page=1247|isbn=978-0-415-24187-8|quote=The welfare state emerged in the twentieth century as one institutional form of this socially protective response. In the 1930s, the responses of emerging welfare states to the Great Depression were to the immediate circumstances of massive unemployment, lost output, and collapse of the financial and trading systems. Planning was not a key element in the response to the crisis of capitalism. Instead the character of welfare state intervention can best be described as an 'interventionist drift', reflecting the spontaneous, uncoordinated reactions of the protective response...By the late 1970s, the welfare state and the capitalist economic structure in which it was placed were in a general state of crisis. There had never been a well articulated vision or ideological foundation of the welfare state.}}</ref> The fullest forms of the welfare state were developed after [[World War II]].<ref name="Béland-2021a"/>

== Etymology ==
The term welfare is much older than the term welfare state. In [[enlightened absolutism]], the ruler had an unlimited position of power, which he was to only utilize to the extent necessary for the "welfare" of his subjects. The content of the "welfare" or "good police", which limited the ruler's legitimate exercise of power, was defined by the authorities at their own discretion. This is also referred to as "welfare absolutism". The term welfare state is used in connection with princely absolutism, this is usually in conjunction with attributes such as [[Absolutism (European history)|absolutist]], [[Mercantilism|mercantilist]] or pre-modern.

The [[German language|German]] term {{lang|de|sozialstaat}}<!--German common nouns not normally capitalized in academic texts, and our manual of style says to avoid unnecessary capitalization--> ("social state") has been used since 1870 to describe state support programs devised by German {{lang|de|[[Historical school of economics|sozialpolitiker]]}} ("social politicians") and implemented as part of [[Otto von Bismarck]]'s conservative reforms.<ref>{{cite journal | first= S. B. | last= Fay | title= Bismarck's Welfare State | journal= Current History | volume= XVIII | date= January 1950 | issue= 101 | pages= 1–7| doi= 10.1525/curh.1950.18.101.1 | s2cid= 249690140 }}</ref>

Today the term is used almost entirely for the "modern" welfare state, which emerged in the 19th century in the course of the socio-economic upheavals caused by [[industrialisation]], the formation of nation states and democratization. While the corresponding English term welfare state is descriptively neutral, the term "{{lang|de|Wohlfahrtsstaat}}" is often used in German as a fighting term with a pejorative connotation.{{Citation needed|date=December 2024}}

The literal English equivalent "social state" did not catch on in Anglophone countries.<ref>{{cite journal |last= Smith |first= Munroe |date= December 1901 |title= Four German Jurists. IV |journal= Political Science Quarterly |volume= 16 |issue= 4 |pages= 641–679 | doi= 10.2307/2140421 |issn= 0032-3195 |jstor= 2140421 }}</ref> However, during the Second World War, Anglican Archbishop [[William Temple (bishop)|William Temple]], author of the book ''Christianity and Social Order'' (1942), popularized the concept using the phrase "welfare state".<ref>{{citation |last= Gough |first= I. |date= 1989 |title= The Welfare State |work= The New Palgrave Social Economics| publisher=New York: W.W. Norton|pages= 276–281 }}</ref> Temple's use of "welfare state" has been connected to [[Benjamin Disraeli]]'s 1845 novel [[Sybil (novel)|''Sybil: or the Two Nations'']] (in other words, the rich and the poor), where he writes "power has only one duty – to secure the social welfare of the PEOPLE".<ref>{{cite book | first= Benjamin | last= Disraeli | author-link= Benjamin Disraeli | chapter-url= http://www.gutenberg.org/files/3760/3760-h/3760-h.htm | title= Sybil | volume = Book 4 | chapter= Chapter 14 | via= [[Project Gutenberg]]}}</ref> At the time he wrote ''Sybil'', Disraeli (later a prime minister) belonged to [[Young England]], a conservative group of youthful [[Tories (British political party)|Tories]] who disagreed with how the [[Whigs (British political party)|Whig]]s dealt with the [[Industrial Revolution#Social effects|conditions of the industrial poor]]. Members of Young England attempted to garner support among the privileged classes to assist the less fortunate and to recognize the [[dignity of labor]] that they imagined had characterized England during the Feudal Middle Ages.<ref>{{cite book | last= Alexander | title= Medievalism | pages= xxiv–xxv, 62, 93, and passim }}</ref>

== History ==
{{See also|Welfare spending#History}}

=== Ancient ===

==== India ====
Emperor [[Ashoka]] of India put forward his idea of a welfare state in the 3rd century [[Common Era|BCE]]. He envisioned his ''[[dharma]]'' (religion or path) as not just a collection of high-sounding phrases.  He consciously tried to adopt it as a matter of state policy; he declared that "all men are my children"<ref>[http://www.cs.colostate.edu/~malaiya/ashoka.html The Edicts of King Asoka], Colostate.</ref> and "whatever exertion I make, I strive only to discharge debt that I owe to all living creatures." It was a completely new ideal of kingship.<ref name= "google592">{{cite book|title=The Penguin History of Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300|year=2003|publisher=Penguin | place = UK|isbn=9780-1-4193742-7|page= 592 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=HqmyEbLScZ4C| first =Romila | last = Thapar |access-date=30 August 2013}}</ref> Ashoka renounced war and conquest by violence and forbade the killing of many animals.<ref name= "google1989">{{cite book |title=Studies in Indian History | issue = 35 | series = Chaukhambha oriental research studies|year= 1989| publisher= Chaukhamba Orientalia | via = The University of Virginia|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=_XlDAAAAYAAJ | first= Upendra |last= Thakur |access-date=30 August 2013}}</ref> Since he wanted to conquer the world through love and faith, he sent many missions to propagate Dharma. Such missions were sent to places like Egypt, Greece, and Sri Lanka. The propagation of Dharma included many measures of people's welfare. Centers of the treatment of men and beasts founded inside and outside of the empire. Shady groves, wells, orchards and rest houses were laid out.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Reddy |first1=Krishna |title=Indian History |date=2011 |page=A-185 |publisher=Tata McGraw Hill |isbn=9780071329231}}</ref> Ashoka also prohibited useless sacrifices and certain forms of gatherings which led to waste, indiscipline and superstition.<ref name="google1989"/> To implement these policies he recruited a new cadre of officers called [[Mahamatra|Dharmamahamattas]]. Part of this group's duties was to see that people of various sects were treated fairly. They were especially asked to look after the welfare of prisoners.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Reddy |first1=Krishna |title=Indian History |date=2011 |pages=A-184–A185 |publisher=Tata McGraw Hill |isbn=9780071329231}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| title= A Text Book of Social Sciences|publisher= Pitambar Publishing|isbn=978-81-209-1466-7|pages=45–46|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=jV6k0FvIC4sC | first1= N. N.| last1= Kher | first2= Jaideep |last2= Aggarwal| via= Google Books}}</ref>

However, the historical record of Ashoka's character is conflicted. Ashoka's own inscriptions state that he converted to [[Buddhism]] after waging a destructive war. However, the Sri Lankan tradition claims that he had already converted to Buddhism in the 4th year of his reign, although it does not mention the conquest of Kalinga.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Seneviratna |first=Anuradha|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iE5uAAAAMAAJ|title=King Aśoka and Buddhism: Historical and Literary Studies|date=1994|publisher= Buddhist Publication Society|isbn= 978-955-24-0065-0}}</ref> During this war, according to [[Edicts of Ashoka|Ashoka's Major Rock Edict 13]], with nearly 100,000 killed in the war and another 150,000 deported. Some sources (particularly Buddhist oral legends) suggest that his conversion was dramatic and that he dedicated the rest of his life to the pursuit of peace and the common good.<ref>{{Cite book|last= Thapar |first=Romila|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pwJuAAAAMAAJ|title=Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas|date=1961|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> However, these sources frequently contradict each other,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Singh|first=Upinder|date=2012|title= Governing the State and the Self: Political Philosophy and Practice in the Edicts of Aśoka|department=South Asian Studies|journal=University of Delhi|volume= 28|issue=2|pages=131–145|doi= 10.1080/02666030.2012.725581|s2cid= 143362618}}</ref> and a few sources (like ''[[Ashokavadana]]'', earliest versions ranging from 200 AD to 500 AD) describe Ashoka engaging in sectarian mass murder throughout his reign, and make no mention of the philanthropic efforts claimed by earlier legends. The interpretation of Ashoka's dharma after conversion is controversial, but in particular, the texts which describe him personally ordering the massacre of Buddhist heretics and Jains have been disputed by many scholars, since these are directly contradictory to his own edicts, and are legendary in nature.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Age Of Impreial Unity|year=1968 |publisher=Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan|pages=234–235|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B1WgAAAAMAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Age Of The Nandas And Mauryas|year=1963 |publisher=Bharatiya Itihas Parishad|url=https://ignca.gov.in/Asi_data/19859.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Danver|first=Steven L.|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=slVobUjdzGMC&pg=RA1-PA99|title=Popular Controversies in World History: Investigating History's Intriguing Questions [4 volumes]: Investigating History's Intriguing Questions|date= 22 December 2010|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-59884-078-0|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Le|first=Huu Phuoc|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9jb364g4BvoC&pg=PA32|title=Buddhist Architecture|date=2010|publisher= Grafikol |isbn=978-0-9844043-0-8}}</ref>

==== China ====
The [[Emperor Wen of Han|Emperor Wen]] (203 – 157 BCE) of [[Han dynasty|Han Dynasty]] instituted a variety of measures with resemblances to modern welfare policies. These included pensions, in the form of food and wine, to all over 80 years of age, as well as monetary support, in the form of loans or tax breaks, to widows, orphans, and elderly without children to support them. Emperor Wen was also known for a concern over wasteful spending of tax-payer money. Unlike other Han emperors, he wore simple silk garments. In order to make the state serve the common people better, cruel criminal punishments were lessened and the state bureaucracy was made more meritocratic. This led to officials being selected by examinations for the first time in Chinese history.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Montgomery|first=Laszlo|title=Han Dynasty (Part 2)|url=https://chinahistorypodcast.libsyn.com/chp-019-the-han-dynasty-part-2|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027055233/https://chinahistorypodcast.libsyn.com/chp-019-the-han-dynasty-part-2|archive-date=27 October 2020|website=[[chinahistorypodcast.libsyn]]}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=October 2024}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Emperor Wendi of Western Han Dynasty|url=https://www.learnchinesehistory.com/emperor-wendi-western-han-dynasty/|website=[[learnchinesehistory]]|date=5 February 2013|access-date=9 August 2021|archive-date=23 May 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220523072005/https://www.learnchinesehistory.com/emperor-wendi-western-han-dynasty/}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=October 2024}}

==== Rome ====
The [[Roman Republic]] intervened sporadically to distribute free or subsidized grain to its population, through the program known as ''[[cura annonae]].'' The city of Rome grew rapidly during the Roman Republic and [[Roman Empire|Empire]], reaching a population approaching one million in the second century AD. The population of the city grew beyond the capacity of the nearby rural areas to meet the food needs of the city.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi= 10.1098/rsif.2017.0367 |pmid = 29142013|pmc = 5721147|title = Urbanism and the division of labour in the Roman Empire|journal = Journal of the Royal Society Interface |volume = 14|issue = 136| article-number = 20170367|year = 2017|last1 = Hanson|first1 = J. W.|last2 = Ortman|first2 = S. G. |last3 = Lobo|first3 = J.}} p. 10.</ref>

Regular grain distribution began in 123 BC with a grain law proposed by [[Gaius Gracchus]] and approved by the Roman [[Plebeian Council]] (popular assembly). The numbers of those receiving free or subsidized grain expanded to a high of an estimated 320,000 people at one point.<ref>{{Cite book | doi=10.1017/CCO9781139025973.019 |chapter = The food supply of the capital|title = The Cambridge Companion to Ancient Rome|pages = 262–277|year = 2013|last1 = Erdkamp|first1 = Paul|isbn = 978-1-13902597-3 |chapter-url=https://www.academia.edu/9021182|publisher=Cambridge University Press}} pp. 262–264.</ref><ref>Cristofori, Alessandro "Grain Distribution on Late Republican Rome," pp 146-151. [https://www.academia.edu/853118/Grain_Distribution_in_Late_Republican_Rome], accessed 17 September 2018</ref> In the 3rd century AD, the dole of grain was replaced by bread, probably during the reign of [[Septimius Severus]] (193–211 AD).  Severus also began providing [[olive oil]] to residents of Rome, and later the emperor [[Aurelian]] (270–275) ordered the distribution of [[wine]] and [[pork]].{{sfn|Erdkamp|2013 |pp=266–267}} The doles of bread, olive oil, wine, and pork apparently continued until near the end of the [[Western Roman Empire]] in 476 AD.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1353/jla.2012.0015 | title=The Roman Grain Supply, 442–455| journal=Journal of Late Antiquity| volume=5| issue=2 | year=2012| last1=Linn| first1= Jason| s2cid=161127852 | pages = 298–321}}.</ref> The dole in the early Roman Empire is estimated to account for 15 to 33 percent of the total grain imported and consumed in Rome.<ref>{{Cite journal |jstor = 4502066 |title = The Organization of the Grain Trade in the Early Roman Empire|journal = The Economic History Review|volume = 60|issue = 2|pages = 313–332|last1 = Kessler|first1 = David|last2 = Temin |first2 = Peter|s2cid = 154086889|year = 2007|doi = 10.1111/j.1468-0289.2006.00360.x}} p. 316.</ref>

In addition to food, the Roman Republic also supplied free entertainment, through ''[[ludi]]'' (public games).  Public money was allocated for the staging of ''ludi,'' but the presiding official increasingly came to augment the splendor of his games from personal funds as a form of [[public relations]]. The sponsor was able to cultivate the favor of the people of [[Rome]].<ref>[[Helen Lovatt]], ''Status and Epic Games: Sport, Politics, and Poetics in the Thebaid'' {{ISBN|978-0-52184742-1}} (Cambridge University Press, 2005), pp. 10</ref>

===Islamic Caliphate===
The concept of states taxing for the welfare budget was introduced to the Arabs in the early 7th century by Caliph [[Umar]], most likely adapted from the newly conquered Roman territories.<ref>Miaschi, John (25 April 2017). [https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-is-a-welfare-state.html  What Is A Welfare State?]  The World Atlas, accessed 24 October 2019.</ref> ''[[Zakat]]'' is also one of the [[five pillars of Islam]] and is a mandatory form of 2.5% [[wealth tax]] to be paid by all individuals holding above a basic threshold ([[nisab]]) to provide for the needy once a year after [[Ramadan]]. [[Umar]] (584–644), leader of the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] (empire), established a welfare state through the [[Bayt al-mal]] (treasury), which for instance was used to stockpile food in every region of the Islamic Empire reserved for Muslims in the Peninsula.<ref name= "Edinburgh">{{cite book| last= Crone|first= Patricia |title= Medieval Islamic Political Thought | publisher= Edinburgh University Press | pages= 308–309 | isbn= 0-7486-2194-6| year= 2005 }}</ref>

=== Modern ===
{{Otto von Bismarck series}}
[[Otto von Bismarck]] established the first welfare state in a modern industrial society, with [[Otto von Bismarck#Social legislation|social-welfare legislation]], in 1880s [[Imperial Germany]].<ref name=Vis>{{cite book|last1=Kersbergen|first1=Kees van|last2=Vis|first2=Barbara|title=Comparative Welfare State Politics: Development, Opportunities, and Reform|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UQL3AQAAQBAJ&pg=PA38|year=2013 |publisher=Cambridge UP|page=38|isbn= 978-1-10765247-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Wimmer|first=Andreas|date= 13 February 2019 |title=Why Nationalism Works|journal= Foreign Affairs: America and the World|language=en-US|url= https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/world/2019-02-12/why-nationalism-works |access-date=30 August 2020|issn= 0015-7120}}</ref> Bismarck extended the privileges of the [[Junker]] social class to ordinary Germans.<ref name=Vis/> His 17 November 1881 Imperial Message to the [[Reichstag (German Empire)|Reichstag]] used the term "practical Christianity" to describe his program.<ref>Moritz Busch, ''Bismarck: Some secret pages from his history,'' Macmillan, New York (1898) Vol. II, p. 282</ref> German laws from this era also insured workers against industrial risks inherent in the workplace.<ref name= Austria>{{cite journal| first= Margarete |last= Grandner| title= Conservative Social Politics in Austria, 1880–1890| journal= Austrian History Yearbook| volume= 27 |year= 1996| pages= 77–107|doi= 10.1017/S006723780000583X|s2cid= 143805293|url= http://purl.umn.edu/90596}}</ref>

In [[Switzerland]], the Swiss Factory Act of 1877 limited working hours for everyone, and gave maternity benefits.<ref name=Austria/>  The [[Public Welfare Policy in Switzerland|Swiss welfare state]] also arose in the late 19th century; its existence and depth varied individually by [[Cantons of Switzerland|canton]]. Some of the programs first adopted were emergency relief, elementary schools, and homes for the elderly and children.<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://www.geschichtedersozialensicherheit.ch/synthese/#c34|title=Geschichte der Sozialen Sicherheit-Synthese |language= de-DE|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref>

In the [[Austro-Hungarian Empire]], a version was set up by Count [[Eduard von Taaffe]] a few years after Bismarck in Germany. Legislation to help the working class in Austria emerged from [[Catholic Church|Catholic]] [[Christian right|conservatives]]. Von Taffe used Swiss and German models of social reform, including the Swiss Factory Act of 1877 German laws that insured workers against industrial risks inherent in the workplace to create the 1885 Trade Code Amendment.<ref name= Austria/>

Changed attitudes in reaction to the worldwide [[Great Depression]] of the 1930s, which brought unemployment and misery to millions, were instrumental in the move to the welfare state in many countries. During the Great Depression, the welfare state was seen as a "middle way" between the extremes of [[communism]] on the left and unregulated ''[[laissez-faire]]'' [[capitalism]] on the right.<ref name="WF EPE">{{cite encyclopedia|year=1999|title=Welfare state|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Political Economy|publisher=Routledge|editor-last=O'Hara|editor-first=Phillip Anthony|page=1245|isbn=978-0-415-24187-8}}</ref> In the period following World War II, some countries in Western Europe moved from partial or selective provision of [[social service]]s to relatively comprehensive "cradle-to-grave" coverage of the population. Other Western European states did not, such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain and France.{{sfn|Esping-Andersen| 1990 |p=108}} Political scientist [[Eileen McDonagh]] has argued that a major determinant of where welfare states arose is whether or not a country had a historical monarchy with familial foundations (a trait that [[Max Weber]] called [[patrimonialism]]); in places where the monarchic state was viewed as a parental steward of the populace, it was easier to shift into a mindset where the industrial state could also serve as a parental steward of the populace.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Eileen |last=McDonagh |author-link=Eileen McDonagh |title=Ripples from the First Wave: The Monarchical Origins of the Welfare State |journal=Perspectives on Politics |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=992–1016 |date=December 2015 |doi=10.1017/S1537592715002273|s2cid=146441936 }}</ref>

The activities of present-day welfare states extend to the provision of both cash welfare benefits (such as old-age pensions or unemployment benefits) and in-kind welfare services (such as health or childcare services). Through these provisions, welfare states can affect the distribution of wellbeing and personal autonomy among their citizens, as well as influencing how their citizens consume and how they spend their time.<ref>{{cite book |last=Esping-Andersen |first=Gøsta |title=Social Foundations of Postindustrial Economies |year=1999 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-874200-5 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Rice |first=James Mahmud |author2=Robert E. Goodin |author3=Antti Parpo  |date=September–December 2006 |title=The Temporal Welfare State: A Crossnational Comparison |journal=Journal of Public Policy |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=195–228 |url=http://www.jamesmahmudrice.info/Welfare.pdf |doi=10.1017/S0143814X06000523 |issn=0143-814X |hdl=10419/31604 |s2cid=38187155 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070615181613/http://www.jamesmahmudrice.info/Welfare.pdf |archive-date=15 June 2007 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Analysis ===
Historian of the 20th-century [[Fascism|fascist movement]], [[Robert Paxton]], observes that the provisions of the welfare state were enacted in the 19th century by [[Christian right|religious conservatives]] to counteract appeals from [[trade union]]s and [[History of socialism|socialism]].<ref name= "Paxton way">{{cite news| first= Robert O.| last= Paxton| title= Vichy Lives! – In a way| url= http://www.nybooks.com:80/articles/archives/2013/apr/25/vichy-lives-in-a-way/?pagination=false| work= The New York Review of Books| date= 25 April 2013| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130414234702/http://www.nybooks.com/articles/archives/2013/apr/25/vichy-lives-in-a-way/?pagination=false| archive-date= 14 April 2013| access-date= 16 May 2020| url-status= live}}</ref> Later, Paxton writes "All the modern twentieth-century European dictatorships of the right, both fascist and authoritarian, were welfare states…  They all provided medical care, pensions, affordable housing, and mass transport as a matter of course, in order to maintain productivity, national unity, and social peace."<ref name= "Paxton way"/> In Germany, [[Adolf Hitler]]'s [[Nazi Party]] maintained the welfare state established by previous German governments, but restructured it so as to help only [[Aryan race|Aryan]] individuals considered worthy of assistance, excluding "alcoholics, tramps, homosexuals, prostitutes, the 'work-shy' or the 'asocial', habitual criminals, the hereditarily ill (a widely defined category) and members of races other than the Aryan."<ref name= Evans>[[Richard J. Evans]], ''The Third Reich in Power, 1933–1939,'' New York: The Penguin Press, 2005, p. 489</ref> Nevertheless, even with these limitations, over 17 million German citizens were receiving assistance under the auspices of the [[Nationalsozialistische Volkswohlfahrt|National Socialist People's Welfare]] by 1939.<ref name=Evans/>

When social democratic parties abandoned [[Marxism]] after [[World War II]], they increasingly accepted the welfare state as a political goal, either as a temporary goal within capitalism or an ultimate goal in itself.<ref name= "Paxton way"/>

A theoretical addition from 2005 is that of Kahl in her article "The religious roots of modern policy: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed Protestant traditions compared." She argues that the welfare state policies of several European countries can be traced back to their religious origins. This process has its origin in the "poor relief" systems, and social norms present in Christian nations. The example countries are categorized as follows: Catholic (Spain, Italy and France); Lutheran (Denmark, Sweden and Germany); Reformed Protestant (Netherlands, the UK and the USA). The Catholic countries had a late adoption of welfare benefits and social assistance, the latter being splintered and meagre, due to several religious and social factors. Giving alms was an important part of Catholic society as the wealthy could resolve their sins through participation in the act. As such, begging was allowed and was subject to a greater degree of acceptance. Poverty was seen as being close to [[Grace in Christianity|grace]], and there was no onus for change placed onto the poor. These factors, coupled with the power of the church meant that state provided benefits did not arise until late in the 20th century. Additionally, social assistance was not done at a comprehensive level, each group in need had its assistance added incrementally. This accounts for the fragmented nature of social assistance in these countries.<ref name="Kahl 91-126">Kahl, Sigrun (2005). ''The religious roots of modern poverty policy: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed Protestant traditions compared.'' European Journal of Sociology, Vol. 46, No. 1, Religion and Society, pp. 91–126.</ref>

Lutheran states were early to provide welfare and late to provide social assistance but this was done uniformly. Poverty was seen as more of an individual affliction of laziness and immorality. Work was viewed as a calling. As such these societies banned begging and created workhouses to force the able-bodied to work. These uniform state actions paved the way for comprehensive welfare benefits, as those who worked deserved assistance when in need. When social assistance was delivered for those who had never worked, it was in the context of the uniform welfare provision. The concept of Predestination is key for understanding welfare assistance in Reformed Protestant states. Poor people were seen as being punished, therefore begging and state assistance was non existent. As such churches and charities filled the void resulting in early social assistance and late welfare benefits. The USA still has minimal welfare benefits today, because of their religious roots, according to Kahl.<ref name="Kahl 91-126"/>

Also from 2005, Jacob Hacker stated that there was "broad agreement" in research on welfare that there had not been welfare state retrenchment. Instead, "social policy frameworks remain secure."<ref>{{cite book|last=Hacker|first= Jacob|title=Beyond Continuity: Institutional Change in Advanced Political Economies|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|chapter=Policy Drift: The Hidden Politics of US Welfare State Retrenchment}}</ref>

== Forms ==
{{see also|Welfare spending#Forms|Social democracy|Christian democracy}}

{{christian Democracy sidebar}}
{{social democracy sidebar}}
{{liberalism sidebar}}
{{progressivism sidebar}}
Broadly speaking, welfare states are either '''universal''', with provisions that cover everybody, or '''selective''', with provisions covering only those deemed most needy. In his 1990 book, ''The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism'', Danish sociologist [[Gøsta Esping-Andersen]] further identified three subtypes of welfare state models: liberal, social-democratic, and conservative.<ref name="Bo Rothstein"/>

Esping-Anderson development of the three subtypes of welfare regimes were categorized under three dimensions: 1) state and market relations or the relationship between the state and market, 2) stratification or social relations and relationships, 3) social citizenship rights or whether or not an individual is dependent on the labor market.<ref name="Esping-Andersen2">{{harvnb|Esping-Andersen|1990|page=228}}</ref>

Since the building of the decommodification index is limited{{efn|According to the French sociologist [[Georges Menahem]], Esping-Andersen's "decommodification index" aggregates both qualitative and quantitative variables for "sets of dimensions" which fluid, and pertain to three very different areas. These characters involve similar limits of the validity of the index and of its potential for replication. Cf. {{harvnb|Menahem|2007}}.}} and the typology is debatable, these 18 countries could be ranked from most purely social-democratic (Sweden) to the most liberal (the United States).<ref name="FS regime">{{cite journal|last1=Ferragina|first1=Emanuele|last2=Seeleib-Kaiser|first2=Martin|year=2011|title=Welfare regime debate: past, present, futures|url=https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01347336/file/Welfare_regime_debate.pdf|journal=Policy & Politics|volume=39|pages=583–611|doi=10.1332/030557311X603592|number=4|s2cid=146986126|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226005038/https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01347336/file/Welfare_regime_debate.pdf|archive-date=26 February 2020|url-status=live }}</ref>{{rp|597}} Ireland represents a near-hybrid model whereby two streams of unemployment benefit exist: contributory and means-tested. However, payments can begin immediately and are theoretically available to all Irish citizens even if they have never worked, provided they are habitually resident.<ref>{{cite news| url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/10391238/Benefits-in-Europe-country-by-country.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/10391238/Benefits-in-Europe-country-by-country.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title= Benefits in Europe: country by country| first= Edward |last= Malnick| date= 19 October 2013| work= The Telegraph}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Social stigma varies across the three conceptual welfare states. Particularly, it is highest in liberal states, and lowest in social democratic states.<ref name="Esping-Andersen" /> Esping-Andersen proposes that the universalist nature of social democratic states eliminate the duality between beneficiaries and non-recipients, whereas in means-tested liberal states there is resentment towards [[Redistribution of income and wealth|redistribution]] efforts. That is to say, the lower the percent of GDP spent on welfare, the higher the stigma of the welfare state.<ref name="Esping-Andersen"/> Esping-Andersen also argues that welfare states set the stage for post-industrial employment evolution in terms of employment growth, structure, and stratification. He uses Germany, Sweden, and the United States to provide examples of the differing results of each of the three welfare states.<ref name="Esping-Andersen"/>

According to Evelyne Huber and John Stephens, different types of welfare states emerged as a result of prolonged government by different parties. They distinguish between social democratic welfare states, Christian democratic welfare states, and "wage earner" states.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Huber|first=Evelyne|title=Development and crisis of the welfare state: parties and policies in global markets|date=2001|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|others=John D. Stephens|isbn=0-226-35646-9|location=Chicago|oclc=45276711}}</ref>

According to the Swedish political scientist [[Bo Rothstein]], in non-universal welfare states, the state is primarily concerned with directing resources to "the people most in need". This requires tight bureaucratic control in order to determine who is eligible for assistance and who is not. Under universal models such as Sweden, on the other hand, the state distributes welfare to all people who fulfill easily established criteria (e.g. having children, receiving medical treatment, etc.) with as little bureaucratic interference as possible. This, however, requires higher taxation due to the scale of services provided. This model was constructed by the Scandinavian ministers [[Karl Kristian Steincke]] and [[Gustav Möller]] in the 1930s and is dominant in Scandinavia.<ref name="Bo Rothstein">[[Bo Rothstein]], ''Just Institutions Matter: the Moral and Political Logic of the Universal Welfare State'' (Cambridge University Press, 1998), pp. 18–27.</ref>

Sociologist [[Lane Kenworthy]] argues that the Nordic experience demonstrates that the modern social democratic model can "promote economic security, expand opportunity, and ensure rising living standards for all ... while facilitating freedom, flexibility and market dynamism."<ref>[[Lane Kenworthy|Kenworthy, Lane]] (2014). ''Social Democratic America''. [[Oxford University Press]]. {{ISBN|0199322511}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=eVTSAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA9 p. 9].</ref>

American political scientist [[Benjamin Radcliff]] has also argued that the universality and generosity of the welfare state (i.e. the extent of [[decommodification]]) is the single most important societal-level structural factor affecting the quality of human life, based on the analysis of time serial data across both the industrial democracies and the American States. He maintains that the welfare state improves life for everyone, regardless of social class (as do similar institutions, such as pro-worker labor market regulations and strong labor unions).<ref>{{cite book| author-link= Benjamin Radcliff| last= Radcliff| first= Benjamin| year= 2013| title= The Political Economy of Human Happiness| place= New York| publisher= Cambridge University Press}}</ref>{{efn|See also [http://benjaminradcliff.com/scholarly-articles/ "this collection of full-text peer-reviewed scholarly articles on this subject"] by Radcliff and colleagues (such as "Social Forces," "The Journal of Politics," and "Perspectives on Politics," among others)}}

=== Gender and welfare ===
Esping-Andersen's welfare typology is often criticized by feminists for being gender blind.<ref name="Nakray-2021">{{Cite journal |last=Nakray |first=Keerty |date=December 2021 |title=Gender, welfare state regimes and social policy beyond advanced capitalism: Pathways to decommodification in middle-income countries |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/spol.12711 |journal=Social Policy & Administration |language=en |volume=55 |issue=7 |pages=1197–1223 |doi=10.1111/spol.12711 |s2cid=233887743 |issn=0144-5596|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to Keerty Nakray, Esping-Andersen's three types of dimensions (state and market relations, stratification, and social citizenship rights) does not acknowledge unpaid care-work done by women within the household economy. This failure of recognizing unpaid work is due to the fact that welfare states are focused on the male-breadwinner concept.<ref name="Nakray-2021" /> Because Esping-Andersen argued that the welfare state set the stage for employment evolution, the lack of gender analysis creates an unintended emphasis on male employment.

Welfare Scholar Peter Dwyer goes further to consider the question of gender and citizenship by showing that it is not gender blind, but citizenship by default is considered masculine, and women are not given citizenship rights.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Dwyer |first=Peter |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt1t89hcn |title=Understanding social citizenship |date=2010-06-09 |edition=second |publisher=Bristol University Press |doi=10.2307/j.ctt1t89hcn |isbn=978-1-4473-4278-6}}</ref> Dwyer explains that citizenship that is considered "male" is seen as "public citizens" who have traits like rationality and impartiality that make them responsible citizens.<ref name=":0" /> On the other hand, Dwyer lays out women's construction of "private non-citizen," where women are the opposite of men, being irrational, emotional, and ill-equipped to handle the responsibilities of citizenship.<ref name=":0" /> This construction of men and women helps explain why citizenship rights and welfare rights are more difficult for women to access. All of these inequities in citizenship rights are only made more intense when other intersectional factors are considered including race, class, sexuality, and education. Dwyer then introduces the concepts of the "caregiver parity model" and the "universal breadwinner model" as ways to allow women easier access to the welfare state. In the caregiver parity model, according to Reid, women have equal access to childcare.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reid |first1=Catherine E. |last2=Moss |first2=Simon |last3=Hyman |first3=Graeme |date=2005-01-01 |title=Caregiver Reciprocity: The effect of reciprocity, carer self-esteem and motivation on the experience of caregiver burden |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00049530500141022 |journal=Australian Journal of Psychology |language=en |volume=57 |issue=3 |pages=186–196 |doi=10.1080/00049530500141022 |issn=0004-9530|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This then allows women to access the labor market freely, offering them the same opportunity as when they receive welfare benefits. On the other hand, the universal breadwinner model, as explained by Lister, focuses less on care work responsibilities and more on women's economic employment opportunities with the belief that access to employment will lead to more equal welfare benefits.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lister |first1=Ruth |chapter=Citizenship and changing welfare states |pages=39–57 |editor1-last=Andersen |editor1-first=Jørgen Goul |editor2-last=Jensen |editor2-first=Per H. |title=Changing Labour Markets, Welfare Policies and Citizenship |isbn=9781861342720 |publisher=Policy Press |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/policy-press-scholarship-online/book/21177/chapter-abstract/180800779 |date=2002-01-23 |doi=10.1332/policypress/9781861342720.003.0003 |access-date=2025-11-11}}</ref> As pointed out by Dwyer, both models allow significant opportunities and challenges for advancing women's welfare citizenship.<ref name=":0" />

Sociologist [[Ann Shola Orloff]] reframes the three dimensions with a gendered lens. As she reframes, Orloff incorporates gender and expands the decommodification index within three dimensions: 1) focus on families and the welfare states in state and market relations, 2) including the relationship between gender and labor in stratifications on social provisions, 3) how men and women are dependent on the labor market and the effect of welfare on decommodification for both genders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Orloff |first=Ann Shola |date=June 1993 |title=Gender and the Social Rights of Citizenship: The Comparative Analysis of Gender Relations and Welfare States |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=303–328 |doi=10.2307/2095903|jstor=2095903 |s2cid=53453651 }}</ref> Reframing the decommodification index with a gendered lens ensures women doing care-work don't get left behind within the welfare state.

=== UBI as a replacement for the welfare state ===
[[Universal basic income]] (UBI) has been proposed as a replacement for the traditional welfare state where social protection schemes are also [[Social policy|social policies]] with a precise aim that can be regarded as [[Social engineering (political science)|social engineering]]. The focus of the UBI is granting individuals more [[freedom]] in determining life choices by providing a lifetime of financial security regardless of one's career preferences or lifepath.<ref>{{Cite web |title="Universal income is more than a new form of welfare state" |url=https://www.polytechnique-insights.com/en/braincamps/economy/has-the-pandemic-revived-debate-over-universal-basic-income/universal-income-is-more-than-just-a-new-form-of-welfare-state/ |access-date=3 April 2023 |website=Polytechnique Insights |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The American conservative political scientist [[Charles Murray (political scientist)|Charles Murray]] has outlined a UBI plan which, in 2014 in the United States of America, would have cost $200 billion less than existing welfare programs. By the year 2020, it would have cost about $1 trillion less.<ref>{{Cite web |last=de Rugy |first=Veronique |date=7 June 2016 |title=Universal Basic Income's Growing Appeal |url=https://www.mercatus.org/economic-insights/expert-commentary/universal-basic-incomes-growing-appeal |access-date=3 April 2023 |website=Mercatus Center}}</ref>

=== Australia ===
{{Further|Social security in Australia}}

Prior to 1900 in Australia, charitable assistance from benevolent societies, sometimes with financial contributions from the authorities, was the primary means of relief for people not able to support themselves.<ref name = abs-1988/> The 1890s economic depression and the rise of the trade unions and the [[Australian Labor Party#History|Labor parties]] during this period led to a movement for welfare reform.<ref name = dict-syd-2008>{{cite web|year= 2008|first= Stephen|last= Garton|title=  Health and welfare|work= The Dictionary of Sydney|access-date= 23 December 2014|url= http://dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/health_and_welfare|url-status= live| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120815071913/http://www.dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/health_and_welfare|archive-date= 15 August 2012}}</ref>

In 1900, New South Wales and Victoria enacted legislation introducing non-contributory pensions for those aged 65 and over. Queensland legislated a similar system in 1907 before the [[Deakin government (1905–1908)|Deakin government]] introduced a national aged pension under the ''Invalid and Old-Aged Pensions Act 1908''. A national invalid disability pension was started in 1910, and a national maternity allowance was introduced by the [[Andrew Fisher|Fisher government]] in 1912.<ref name = abs-1988>{{cite web|year= 1988|title= History of Pensions and Other Benefits in Australia| work= Year Book Australia, 1988  |publisher= Australian Bureau of Statistics|access-date= 23 December 2014|url= http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/3d68c56307742d8fca257090002029cd/8e72c4526a94aaedca2569de00296978!OpenDocument|url-status= live|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141223142853/http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/3d68c56307742d8fca257090002029cd/8e72c4526a94aaedca2569de00296978!OpenDocument|archive-date= 23 December 2014}}</ref><ref name = australia-wr-2000/>

In the 1920s and 1930s, detailed proposals were developed for [[National Insurance (Australia)|a comprehensive national insurance scheme]] covering medical, disability, unemployment and pension benefits. Multiple royal commissions were held on the subject and the scheme was legislated as the ''[[National Health and Pensions Insurance Act 1938]]''. However, the scheme was ultimately abandoned for cost reasons in the lead-up to the Second World War.<ref>{{cite book |first=James |last=Gillespie |year=1991 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge |title=The Price of Health: Australian Governments and Medical Politics 1910–1960 |oclc=49638492 |isbn=978-0-521-52322-6|pages=91–99}}</ref>

During the Second World War, the federal government created a welfare state by enacting national schemes for: child endowment in 1941; a widows' pension in 1942; a wife's allowance in 1943; additional allowances for the children of pensioners in 1943; and unemployment, sickness, and special benefits in 1945.<ref name = abs-1988/><ref name=australia-wr-2000>{{cite web|date=September 2000 |first=Peter|last=Yeend|title=Welfare Review|publisher=Parliament of Australia|access-date=23 December 2014| url= http://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/Publications_Archive/archive/welfarebrief| url-status= live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141223134852/http://www.peeep.us/2cbb82ee|archive-date=23 December 2014}}</ref>

[[Medicare (Australia)|Medicare]] is Australia's publicly funded universal health care insurance scheme. Initially created in 1975 by the [[Whitlam]] Labor government under the name "Medibank". The Fraser Liberal government made significant changes to it from 1976 leading to its abolition in late 1981. The Hawke government reinstated universal health care in 1984 under the name "Medicare".

=== Brunei ===
[[Brunei]] operates a comprehensive welfare state, primarily funded by its substantial oil and gas revenues, which account for approximately 65% of its GDP and 90% of government income. This wealth enables the government to provide citizens with extensive benefits, including free education, free or heavily subsidized healthcare, public housing, and various subsidies on essential goods like fuel and food. Notably, Bruneians pay no personal [[income tax]], and the state covers many living expenses.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hashim |first1=Hafiizh |last2=Druce |first2=Stephen C. |last3=Julay |first3=Abdul Hai |title=Brunei Darussalam's Economic Transition in a Shifting Global Asia |chapter=Brunei Darussalam's Economic Diversification Drive: An Assessment of the Socioeconomic and Geopolitical Issues and Challenges. Overcoming Path Dependence? |series=Asia in Transition |date=2025 |volume=23 |pages=21–38 |doi=10.1007/978-981-97-6926-1_2|isbn=978-981-97-6925-4 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

However, Brunei's heavy reliance on [[hydrocarbon resources]] poses sustainability challenges, especially amid global shifts toward [[renewable energy]]. Recognizing this, the government has initiated economic diversification efforts under the "Wawasan Brunei 2035" vision, aiming to reduce dependence on oil and gas by developing sectors like technology, tourism, and agriculture. Despite these initiatives, progress has been gradual, and the long-term viability of Brunei's welfare model remains contingent on successful economic transformation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bakar |first1=Rasidah Hj Abu |title=Brunei sets goals for diversifying economy beyond oil |url=https://thescoop.co/2021/01/08/brunei-sets-goals-for-diversifying-economy-beyond-oil/ |website=The Scoop |access-date=28 April 2025 |date=8 January 2021}}</ref>

=== Canada ===
Canada's [[Social programs in Canada|welfare programs]]<ref name="Canada">[https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/programs/communities/reports/welfare-income-2009/chapter1.html Chapter 1: What is Welfare?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306044624/https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/programs/communities/reports/welfare-income-2009/chapter1.html |date=6 March 2019 }} Retrieved: 4 March 2019.</ref> are funded and administered at all levels of government (with 13 different<ref name="Canada"/> provincial/territorial systems), and include health and medical care, public education (through graduate school), social housing and social services. Social support is given through programs including Social Assistance, Guaranteed Income Supplement, Child Tax Benefit, Old Age Security, Employment Insurance, Workers' Compensation, and the Canada/Quebec Pension Plans.<ref>[https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/welfare-state Welfare State.] Retrieved: 4 March 2019.</ref>

=== China ===
{{main|Social welfare in China}}

China traditionally relied on the extended family to provide welfare services.<ref>{{cite book| first1= A. B. |last1= Susanto | first2= Patricia |last2= Susanto|title= The Dragon Network: Inside Stories of the Most Successful Chinese Family Businesses|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=xq18xB7SpPgC&pg=PA22|year= 2013|publisher= Wiley|page=22|isbn= 978-1-11833938-1}}</ref> The [[one-child policy]] introduced in 1978 has made that unrealistic, and new models have emerged since the 1980s as China has rapidly become richer and more urban. Much discussion is underway regarding China's proposed path toward a welfare state.<ref>{{cite book| first = Scott | last = Kennedy|title= Beyond the Middle Kingdom: Comparative Perspectives on China's Capitalist Transformation|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=p_5D_eElygkC&pg=PA89|year= 2011|publisher= Stanford U.P.|page= 89|isbn= 978-0-80477767-4}}</ref> Chinese policies have been incremental and fragmented in terms of social insurance, privatization, and targeting. In the cities, where the rapid economic development has centered, lines of cleavage have developed between state-sector and non-state-sector employees, and between labor-market insiders and outsiders.<ref>{{cite journal| first= Xian |last= Huang|s2cid= 18306913| title= The Politics of Social Welfare Reform in Urban China: Social Welfare Preferences and Reform Policies| journal= Journal of Chinese Political Science |date= March 2013| volume= 18| number= 1| pages= 61–85|doi= 10.1007/s11366-012-9227-x|url= https://scholarship.libraries.rutgers.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/The-Politics-of-Social-Welfare-Reform/991031550236404646}}</ref>
